title: Where prayer comes from (CCC 2652–2660)
hookLine: the word, the liturgy, faith, hope, charity, and today

cards: Turn on a kitchen tap and water comes out. Simple. Except the water didn't start in the kitchen.
Somewhere out of sight there's a reservoir, a main under the street, a pipe in the wall. The tap is only where it shows up. The Catechism asks the same about prayer.
If prayer is speaking with God, where does the speaking come from? It names a handful of springs, and the last one on its list is so plain it's easy to miss. Today: where prayer comes from.

teach.b: The Catechism begins back at the well from a few days ago, where Jesus promises water that, in the Douay-Rheims, "shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting."

It reads that living water as the Holy Spirit, then asks where we go to draw it. First spring: the word of God. It recalls Saint Ambrose: when we pray, we speak to God; when we read the scriptures, we hear him.

Second: the liturgy. At Mass and in the Church's daily prayer, the Church prays together, and personal prayer takes that liturgy in and makes it its own, during the celebration and after it. Third: three virtues.
Faith, which it calls the way in.
Hope, in Paul's words: "hope confoundeth not: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts." And charity, love itself. Then the surprise.
The last spring isn't a book or a building. It's today. The Catechism points to a psalm: "To day if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts."
We learn to pray at certain moments, it says, but the Spirit is offered at all times, in the events of each day. A traffic jam. A waiting room.
A child's question over cereal. In this reading, those aren't interruptions of prayer. They're where it can spring up.

how: Catholics draw their prayer from reading scripture, from the Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours, and from the events of an ordinary day, which some bring to God as they happen.

games.q: what does “where prayer comes from” mean?
o: the church building where prayer must take place
the set hours when Catholics are told to pray
the springs prayer draws on, from scripture to today

s: the Catechism says prayer comes only from set prayer times
it says we learn at certain moments, but the Spirit is offered at all times, in the events of each day.

games.q: you sit down to pray and nothing comes. by today's teaching, where can you start?
o: wait until you feel holy enough.
start with what's in front of you today.
games.why: the last spring on the Catechism's list is today: the Spirit is offered in the events of each day, so the day itself is a place to begin.

practice: Don't reach for a holy thought; look at what's actually here: the chair under you, a sound in the next room, something on your mind for later. Pick one.
If you pray, bring it to God just as it is, in a sentence of your own; if you don't, simply notice it fully, without fixing it.

wordCard.voice: Where prayer comes from. In the Catechism, the springs prayer draws on: the word of God, the liturgy, faith, hope and charity, and today itself.

orig.note: Hebrew: today — the word that opens the psalm line "to day if you shall hear his voice" (Psalm 95 in Hebrew numbering, 94 in the Douay-Rheims).

carryVoice: Your line: today is a source. The plainest spring is the one you're standing in. See you tomorrow.
